entries.083b6368bd9be42b40e54bf7d6b34f23afec57e2: <div sID="gen2326" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Lev.8" sID="Lev.8"/> <div eID="gen2326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2327" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2328" type="x-p"/> This chapter gives us an account of the solemn consecration of Aaron and his sons to the priest's office. I. It was done publicly, and the congregation was called together to be witnesses of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.1-Lev.8.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. It was done exactly according to God's appointment, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.5">ver. 5</reference>. 1. They were washed and dressed, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.6-Lev.8.9">ver. 6-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.13">13</reference>. 2. The tabernacle and the utensils of it were anointed, and then the priests, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.10-Lev.8.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. 3. A sin-offering was offered for them, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.14-Lev.8.17">ver. 14-17</reference>. 4. A burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.18-Lev.8.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. 5. The ram of consecration, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.22-Lev.8.30">ver. 22-30</reference>. 6. The continuance of this solemnity for seven days, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.31-Lev.8.36">ver. 31</reference>, &c.
entries.eff317a77cf4611d64d6fbe168640b6af4df21cb: <div eID="gen2328" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2327" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Consecration of Aaron and His Sons. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2329" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments, and the anointing oil, and a bullock for the sin offering, and two rams, and a basket of unleavened bread; 3 And gather thou all the congregation together unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Moses did as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded him; and the assembly was gathered together unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Moses said unto the congregation, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the thing which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded to be done. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Moses brought Aaron and his sons, and washed them with water. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he put upon him the coat, and girded him with the girdle, and clothed him with the robe, and put the ephod upon him, and he girded him with the curious girdle of the ephod, and bound <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto him therewith. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he put the breastplate upon him: also he put in the breastplate the Urim and the Thummim. 9 And he put the mitre upon his head; also upon the mitre, <hi type="italic">even</hi> upon his forefront, did he put the golden plate, the holy crown; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Moses took the anointing oil, and anointed the tabernacle and all that <hi type="italic">was</hi> therein, and sanctified them. 11 And he sprinkled thereof upon the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all his vessels, both the laver and his foot, to sanctify them. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he poured of the anointing oil upon Aaron's head, and anointed him, to sanctify him. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Moses brought Aaron's sons, and put coats upon them, and girded them with girdles, and put bonnets upon them; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <div eID="gen2329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2330" type="x-p"/> God had given Moses orders to consecrate Aaron and his sons to the priests' office, when he was with him the first time upon Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Exod.28.1-Exod.29.46">Exod. xxviii. and xxix.</reference>, where we have also the particular instructions he had how to do it. Now here we have, <div eID="gen2330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2331" type="x-p"/> I. The orders repeated. What was there commanded to be done is here commanded to be done <hi type="italic">now,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.8.2-Lev.8.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. The tabernacle was newly set up, which, without the priests, would be as a candlestick without a candle; the law concerning sacrifices was newly given, but could not be observed without priests; for, though Aaron and his sons had been nominated to the office, they could not officiate, till they were consecrated, which yet must not be done till the place of their ministration was prepared, and the ordinances were instituted, that they might apply themselves to work as soon as ever they were consecrated, and might know that they were ordained, not only to the honour and profit, but to the business of the priesthood. Aaron and his sons were near relations to Moses, and therefore he would not consecrate them till he had further orders, lest he should seem too forward to bring honour into his family. <div eID="gen2331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2332" type="x-p"/> II. The congregation called together, <hi type="italic">at the door,</hi> that is, in the court <hi type="italic">of the tabernacle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.8.4">v. 4</reference>. The elders and principal men of the congregation, who represented the body of the people, were summoned to attend; for the court would hold but a few of the many thousands of Israel. It was done thus publicly, 1. Because it was a solemn transaction between God and Israel; the priests were to be <hi type="italic">ordained for men in things pertaining to God,</hi> for the maintaining of a settled correspondence, and the negotiating of all affairs between the people and God; and therefore it was fit that both sides should appear, to own the appointment, at the door of the tabernacle of meeting. 2. The spectators of the solemnity could not but be possessed, by the sight of it, with a great veneration for the priests and their office, which was necessary among a people so wretchedly prone as these were to envy and discontent. It was strange that any of those who were witnesses of what was here done should afterwards say, as some of them did, <hi type="italic">You take too much upon you, you sons of Levi;</hi> but what would they have said if it had been done clandestinely? Note, It is very fit, and of good use, that ministers should be ordained publicly, <hi type="italic">plebe praesente—in the presence of the common people,</hi> according to the usage of the primitive church. <div eID="gen2332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2333" type="x-p"/> III. The commission read, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.5">v. 5</reference>. Moses, who was God's representative in this solemnity, produced his orders before the congregation: <hi type="italic">This is the thing which the Lord commanded to be done.</hi> Though God had crowned him king in Jeshurun, when he made his face to shine in the sight of all Israel, yet he did not institute or appoint any thing in God's worship but what God himself had commanded. The priesthood he delivered to them was that which he had received from the Lord. Note, All that minister about holy things must have an eye to God's command as their rule and warrant; for it is only in the observance of this that they can expect to be owned and accepted of God. Thus we must be able to say, in all acts of religious worship, <hi type="italic">This is the thing which the Lord commanded to be done.</hi> <div eID="gen2333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2334" type="x-p"/> IV. The ceremony performed according to the divine ritual. 1. Aaron and his sons were <hi type="italic">washed with water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.6">v. 6</reference>), to signify that they ought now to purify themselves from all sinful dispositions and inclinations, and ever after to keep themselves pure. Christ washes those from their sins in his own blood whom he makes to our God kings and priests (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.5-Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 5, 6</reference>); and those that draw near to God must be washed in pure water, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">Heb. x. 22</reference>. Though they were ever so clean before and no filth was to be seen upon them, yet they must be washed, to signify their purification from sin, with which their souls were polluted, how clean soever their bodies were. 2. They were clothed with the holy garments, Aaron with his (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.7-Lev.8.9">v. 7-9</reference>), which typified the dignity of Christ our great high priest, and his sons with theirs (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.13">v. 13</reference>), which typified the decency of Christians, who are spiritual priests. Christ wears the breast-plate of judgment and the holy crown; for the church's high priest is her prophet and king. All believers are clothed with the robe of righteousness, and girt with the girdle of truth, resolution, and close application; and their heads are <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> as the word here is, with the bonnet or diadem of beauty, the beauty of holiness. 3. The high priest was anointed, and, it should seem, the holy things were anointed at the same time; some think that they were anointed before, but that the anointing of them is mentioned here because Aaron was anointed with the same oil with which they were anointed; but the manner of relating it here makes it more than probable that it was done at the same time, and that the seven days employed in consecrating the altar were coincident with the seven days of the priests' consecration. The tabernacle, and all its utensils, had some of the anointing oil put upon them with Moses's finger (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.10">v. 10</reference>), so had the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.11">v. 11</reference>); these were to sanctify the gold and the gift (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.17-Matt.23.19">Matt. xxiii. 17-19</reference>), and therefore must themselves be thus sanctified; but he poured it out more plentifully upon the head of Aaron (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.12">v. 12</reference>), so that it ran down to the <hi type="italic">skirts of his garments,</hi> because his unction was to typify the anointing of Christ with the Spirit, which was not given by measure to him. Yet all believers also have received the anointing, which puts an indelible character upon them, <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1 John ii. 27</reference>.
entries.c4f39c8ffd421e1f2fb350aac8938e0227ae9afb: <div eID="gen2334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2335" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And he brought the bullock for the sin offering: and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon the head of the bullock for the sin offering. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he slew <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and Moses took the blood, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the horns of the altar round about with his finger, and purified the altar, and poured the blood at the bottom of the altar, and sanctified it, to make reconciliation upon it. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he took all the fat that <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the inwards, and the caul <hi type="italic">above</hi> the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the altar. <hi type="super">17</hi> But the bullock, and his hide, his flesh, and his dung, he burnt with fire without the camp; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he brought the ram for the burnt offering: and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon the head of the ram. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he killed <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and Moses sprinkled the blood upon the altar round about. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he cut the ram into pieces; and Moses burnt the head, and the pieces, and the fat. <hi type="super">21</hi> And he washed the inwards and the legs in water; and Moses burnt the whole ram upon the altar: it <hi type="italic">was</hi> a burnt sacrifice for a sweet savour, <hi type="italic">and</hi> an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">22</hi> And he brought the other ram, the ram of consecration: and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon the head of the ram. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he slew <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and Moses took of the blood of it, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot. <hi type="super">24</hi> And he brought Aaron's sons, and Moses put of the blood upon the tip of their right ear, and upon the thumbs of their right hands, and upon the great toes of their right feet: and Moses sprinkled the blood upon the altar round about. <hi type="super">25</hi> And he took the fat, and the rump, and all the fat that <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the inwards, and the caul <hi type="italic">above</hi> the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and the right shoulder: <hi type="super">26</hi> And out of the basket of unleavened bread, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he took one unleavened cake, and a cake of oiled bread, and one wafer, and put <hi type="italic">them</hi> on the fat, and upon the right shoulder: <hi type="super">27</hi> And he put all upon Aaron's hands, and upon his sons' hands, and waved them <hi type="italic">for</hi> a wave offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">28</hi> And Moses took them from off their hands, and burnt <hi type="italic">them</hi> on the altar upon the burnt offering: they <hi type="italic">were</hi> consecrations for a sweet savour: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">29</hi> And Moses took the breast, and waved it <hi type="italic">for</hi> a wave offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">for</hi> of the ram of consecration it was Moses' part; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Moses took of the anointing oil, and of the blood which <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the altar, and sprinkled <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon Aaron, <hi type="italic">and</hi> upon his garments, and upon his sons, and upon his sons' garments with him; and sanctified Aaron, <hi type="italic">and</hi> his garments, and his sons, and his sons' garments with him. <div eID="gen2335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2336" type="x-p"/> The covenant of priesthood must be made by sacrifice, as well as other covenants, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">Ps. l. 5</reference>. And thus Christ was consecrated by the sacrifice of himself, once for all. Sacrifices of each kind must be offered for the priests, that they might with the more tenderness and concern offer the gifts and sacrifices of the people, with compassion on the ignorant, and on <hi type="italic">those that were out of the way,</hi> not insulting over those for whom sacrifices were offered, remembering that they themselves had had sacrifices offered for them, being <hi type="italic">compassed with infirmity.</hi> 1. A bullock, the largest sacrifice, was offered for a sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.14">v. 14</reference>), that hereby atonement might be made, and they might not bring any of the guilt of the sins of their former state into the new character they were now to put on. When Isaiah was sent to be a prophet, he was told to his comfort, <hi type="italic">Thy iniquity is taken away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.7">Isa. vi. 7</reference>. Ministers, that are to declare the remission of sins to others, should give diligence to get it made sure to themselves in the first place that their own sins are pardoned. Those to whom is <hi type="italic">committed the ministry of reconciliation</hi> must first be reconciled to God themselves, that they may deal for the souls of others as for their own. 2. A ram was offered for a burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.18-Lev.8.21">v. 18-21</reference>. By this they gave to God the glory of this great honour which was now put upon them, and returned him praise for it, as Paul thanked Christ Jesus for <hi type="italic">putting him into the ministry,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1 Tim. i. 12</reference>. They also signified the devoting of themselves and all their services to the honour of God. 3. Another ram, called the <hi type="italic">ram of consecration,</hi> was offered for a peace-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.22">v. 22</reference>, &c. The blood of it was part put on the priests, on their ears, thumbs, and toes, and part sprinkled upon the altar; and thus he did (as it were) marry them to the altar, upon which they must all their days give attendance. All the ceremonies about this offering, as those before, were appointed by the express command of God; and, if we compare this chapter with <reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.46">Exod. xxix</reference>, we shall find that the performance of the solemnity exactly agrees with the precept there, and in nothing varies. Here, therefore, as in the account we had of the tabernacle and its vessels, it is again and again repeated, <hi type="italic">As the Lord commanded Moses.</hi> And thus Christ, when he sanctified himself with his own blood, had an eye to his Father's will in it. <hi type="italic">As the Father gave me commandment so I do,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.31">John xiv. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.18">x. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.38">vi. 38</reference>.
entries.cf1dc4ed24d3381c3f070840014e6e674c090416: <div eID="gen2336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2337" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And Moses said unto Aaron and to his sons, Boil the flesh <hi type="italic">at</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation: and there eat it with the bread that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the basket of consecrations, as I commanded, saying, Aaron and his sons shall eat it. <hi type="super">32</hi> And that which remaineth of the flesh and of the bread shall ye burn with fire. <hi type="super">33</hi> And ye shall not go out of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation <hi type="italic">in</hi> seven days, until the days of your consecration be at an end: for seven days shall he consecrate you. <hi type="super">34</hi> As he hath done this day, <hi type="italic">so</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath commanded to do, to make an atonement for you. <hi type="super">35</hi> Therefore shall ye abide <hi type="italic">at</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation day and night seven days, and keep the charge of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that ye die not: for so I am commanded. <hi type="super">36</hi> So Aaron and his sons did all things which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded by the hand of Moses. <div eID="gen2337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2338" type="x-p"/> Moses, having done his part of the ceremony, now leaves Aaron and his sons to do theirs. <div eID="gen2338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2339" type="x-p"/> I. They must boil the flesh of their peace-offering, and eat it in the court of the tabernacle, and what remained they must burn with fire, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.31-Lev.8.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. This signified their thankful consent to the consecration: when God gave Ezekiel his commission, he told him to eat the roll, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.1-Ezek.3.2">Ezek. iii. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen2339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2340" type="x-p"/> II. They must not stir out of the court of the tabernacle for seven days, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.33">v. 33</reference>. The priesthood being a good warfare, they must thus learn to endure hardness, and to disentangle themselves from the affairs of this life, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3-2Tim.2.4">2 Tim. ii. 3, 4</reference>. Being consecrated to their service, they must <hi type="italic">give themselves wholly to it,</hi> and <hi type="italic">attend continually to this very thing.</hi> Thus Christ's apostles were appointed to <hi type="italic">wait for the promise of the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.4">Acts i. 4</reference>. During this time appointed for their consecration, they were daily to repeat the same sacrifices which were offered the first day, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.34">v. 34</reference>. This shows the imperfection of the legal sacrifices, which, because they could not take away sin, were often repeated (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.1-Heb.10.2">Heb. x. 1, 2</reference>), but were here repeated seven times (a number of perfection), because they typified that <hi type="italic">one offering, which perfected for ever those that were sanctified.</hi> The work lasted seven days; for it was a kind of creation: and this time was appointed in honour of the sabbath, which, probably, was the last day of the seven, for which they were to prepare during the six days. Thus the time of our life, like the six days, must be our preparation for the perfection of our consecration to God in the everlasting sabbath: they attended <hi type="italic">day and night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.35">v. 35</reference>), and so constant should we be in our meditation on God's law, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Ps. i. 2</reference>. They attended to <hi type="italic">keep the charge of the Lord:</hi> we have every one of us a charge to keep, an eternal God to glorify, an immortal soul to provide for, needful duty to be done, our generation to serve; and it must be our daily care to keep this charge, for it is the charge of the Lord our Master, who will shortly call us to an account about it, and it is at our utmost peril if we neglect it. Keep it <hi type="italic">that you die not;</hi> it is death, eternal death, to betray the trust we are charged with; by the consideration of this we must be kept in awe. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> We are told (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.36">v. 36</reference>) that <hi type="italic">Aaron and his sons did all that was commanded.</hi> Thus their consecration was completed; and thus they set an example before the people of an exact obedience to the laws of sacrifices now newly given, and then they could with the better grace teach them. Thus the <hi type="italic">covenant of peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.25.12">Num. xxv. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">of life and peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.5">Mal. ii. 5</reference>), was made with Aaron and his sons; but after all the ceremonies that were used in their consecration there was one point of ratification which was reserved to be the honour and establishment of Christ's priesthood, which was this, that they were <hi type="italic">made priests without an oath, but Christ with an oath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.7.21">Hab. vii. 21</reference>), for neither such priests nor their priesthood could continue, but Christ's is a perpetual and unchangeable priesthood. <div eID="gen2340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2341" type="x-p"/> Gospel ministers are compared to those who served at the altar, for they <hi type="italic">minister about holy things</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">1 Cor. ix. 13</reference>), they are God's mouth to the people and the people's to God, the pastors and teachers Christ has appointed to continue in the church to the end of the world: they seem to be meant in that promise which points at gospel times (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">Isa. lvi. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will take of them for priests and for Levites.</hi> No man may take this honour to himself, but he who upon trial is found to be clothed and anointed by the Spirit of God with gifts and graces to qualify him for it, and who with purpose of heart devotes himself entirely to the service, and is then by the <hi type="italic">word and prayer</hi> (for so every thing is sanctified), and the imposition of the hands of those that <hi type="italic">give themselves to the word and prayer,</hi> set apart to the office, and recommended to Christ as a servant and to the church as a steward and guide. And those that are thus solemnly dedicated to God ought not to depart from his service, but faithfully to abide in it all their days; and those that do so, and continue <hi type="italic">labouring in the word and doctrine,</hi> are to be accounted <hi type="italic">worthy of double honour,</hi> double to that of the Old-Testament priests.  <chapter eID="Lev.8"/> <div eID="gen2341" type="x-p"/>

entries.a58684347910333ace25c981750687355b822b65: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1036"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.8.1-Lev.8.36">Le 8:1-36</reference>. Moses Consecrates Aaron and His Sons.</title> <div sID="gen1427" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1036"/><hi type="bold">2. Take Aaron and his sons--</hi>The consecration of Aaron and his sons had been ordered long before (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.46">Ex 29:1-46</reference>), but it is now described with all the details of the ceremonial, as it was gone through after the tabernacle was completed and the regulations for the various sacrifices enacted. <div eID="gen1427" type="x-p"/>
entries.958d694b00eb762cfe62b870609ac3e37b2b4d36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1037"/><div sID="gen1428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1037"/><hi type="bold">3-5. gather thou all the congregation together, &c.--</hi>It was manifestly expedient for the Israelitish people to be satisfied that Aaron's appointment to the high dignity of the priesthood was not a personal intrusion, nor a family arrangement between him and Moses; and nothing, therefore, could be a more prudent or necessary measure, for impressing a profound conviction of the divine origin and authority of the priestly institution, than to summon a general assembly of the people, and in their presence perform the solemn ceremonies of inauguration, which had been prescribed by divine authority. <div eID="gen1428" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b701d17f7ecf79309e4cb3c5600bbc6161e957b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1038"/><div sID="gen1429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1038"/><hi type="bold">6. Moses ... washed them with water--</hi>At consecration they were subjected to entire ablution, though on ordinary occasions they were required, before entering on their duties, only to wash their hands and feet. This symbolical ablution was designed to teach them the necessity of inward purity, and the imperative obligation on those who bore the vessels and conducted the services of the sanctuary to be holy. <div eID="gen1429" type="x-p"/>
entries.884c3f0e428f55a6ecce613e1a37ff06d417becc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1039"/><div sID="gen1430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1039"/><hi type="bold">7-9. he put upon him the coat, and girded him with the girdle--</hi>The splendor of the official vestments, together with the gorgeous tiara of the high priest, was intended, doubtless, in the first instance, to produce in the minds of the people a high respect for the ministers of religion; and in the next, from the predominant use of linen, to inculcate upon Aaron and his sons the duty of maintaining unspotted righteousness in their characters and lives. <div eID="gen1430" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3f48c99f43e25470873a089005c55c8bf76d9be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1040"/><div sID="gen1431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1040"/><hi type="bold">10-12. took the anointing oil, &c.--</hi>which was designed to intimate that persons who acted as leaders in the solemn services of worship should have the unction of the Holy One both in His gifts and graces. <div eID="gen1431" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1a529db6222b355cb585fd1df027255fbd7db77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1041"/><div sID="gen1432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1041"/><hi type="bold">14-17. brought the bullock for the sin offering, &c.--</hi>a timely expression of their sense of unworthiness--a public and solemn confession of their personal sins and a transference of their guilt to the typical victim. <div eID="gen1432" type="x-p"/>
entries.d529127f0d5a83b0ad633bc49fbe453f4eb139b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1042"/><div sID="gen1433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1042"/><hi type="bold">18-21. brought the ram, &c.--</hi>as a token of their entire dedication to the service of God. <div eID="gen1433" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8cca88e7a8f5b3fd11e1ab01f2cf7943a3a50f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1043"/><div sID="gen1434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1043"/><hi type="bold">22-30. brought the other ram,--</hi>&c. After the sin offering and burnt offering had been presented on their behalf, this was their peace offering, by which they declared the pleasure which they felt in entering upon the service of God and being brought into close communion with Him as the ministers of His sanctuary, together with their confident reliance on His grace to help them in all their sacred duties. <div eID="gen1434" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5510d0531808647eb28bc70d2d1905a18929895: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1044"/><div sID="gen1435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1044"/><hi type="bold">33. ye shall not go out of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, &c.--</hi>After all these preliminaries, they had still to undergo a week's probation in the court of the tabernacle before they obtained permission to enter into the interior of the sacred building. During the whole of that period the same sacrificial rites were observed as on the first day, and they were expressly admonished that the smallest breach of any of the appointed observances would lead to the certain forfeiture of their lives [Le 8:35]. <chapter eID="Lev.8"/>

entries.2dbeed7c449b824d2e6e9c9b224092cbfc3ef067: <div eID="gen4457" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4458" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4459" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4459" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4458" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4460" type="x-p"/> Moses is commanded to consecrate Aaron and his sons, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.1-Lev.8.3">Lev 8:1-3</reference>. Moses convenes the congregation; washes, clothes, and anoints Aaron, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.4-Lev.8.12">Lev 8:4-12</reference>. He also clothes Aaron's sons, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.13">Lev 8:13</reference>. Offers a bullock for them as a sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.14-Lev.8.17">Lev 8:14-17</reference>. And a ram for a burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.18-Lev.8.21">Lev 8:18-21</reference>. And another ram for a consecration-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.22-Lev.8.24">Lev 8:22-24</reference>. The fat, with cakes of unleavened bread, and the right shoulder of the ram, he offers as a wave-offering, and afterwards burns, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.25-Lev.8.28">Lev 8:25-28</reference>. The breast, which was the part of Moses, he also waves, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.29">Lev 8:29</reference>. And sprinkles oil and blood upon Aaron and his sons, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.30">Lev 8:30</reference>. The flesh of the consecration ram is to be boiled and eaten at the door of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.31">Lev 8:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.32">Lev 8:32</reference>. Moses commands Aaron and his sons to abide seven days at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, which they do accordingly, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.33-Lev.8.36">Lev 8:33-36</reference>.
entries.931d18d4cf30e7c769128150aed93a575eeca933: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4461" type="x-p"/> Take Aaron and his sons - The whole subject of this chapter has been anticipated in the notes, <reference osisRef="Exo.28.1">Exo 28:1</reference> (note), etc., and <reference osisRef="Exo.29.1">Exo 29:1</reference> (note), etc., in which all the sacrifices, rites, and ceremonies have been explained in considerable detail; and to those notes the reader is referred. It is only necessary to observe that Aaron and his sons were not anointed until now. Before, the thing was commanded; now, first performed.

entries.57ad8b0a5400255c9bf2204250b851f0e098392a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen4464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4465" type="x-p"/> Put it upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, etc. - See this significant ceremony explained in the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.20">Exo 29:20</reference> (note). Calmet remarks that the consecration of the high priest among the Romans bore a considerable resemblance to the consecration of the Jewish high priest. "The Roman priest, clothed with a garment of silk, his head covered with a crown of gold adorned with sacred ribbons, was conducted into a subterranean place, over which there was a floor of planks pierced through with many holes. On this floor they sacrificed a bullock, whose blood was freely poured out on the planks or floor, which running through the holes fell upon the priest, who stood under to receive this sacred aspersion, and who, in order to be completely covered with the blood, took care to present the whole of his body, his clothes, face, eyes, nose, lips, and even his tongue, to receive the drops of blood falling through the pierced floor above. Being completely covered with this sanguineous shower, he ascended from his subterranean place, and was acknowledged and adored by the people as Pontifex Maximus, or supreme high priest." These rites, which bear a striking allusion to those used in the consecration of Aaron, and from which they were probably borrowed, and disguised by the introduction of their own superstitions, are particularly described by Aurelius Prudentius, in his poem entitled Romani Martyris Supplicium, from which I shall select those verses, the subject of which is given above, as the passage is curious, and the work not common. entries.3d4d19aaceb541abadb6a2572da56b3a7613d30c: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4529" type="x-p"/> And waved them for a wave-offering - See the nature of this and the heave-offering in the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference> (note).
entries.7f9b8e410487f5c1682c1c1dfc9192af24be9bfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen4529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4530" type="x-p"/> And Moses took - the blood - and sprinkled it upon Aaron, etc. - Thus we find that the high priest himself must be sprinkled with the blood of the sacrifice; and our blessed Lord, of whom Aaron was a type, was sprinkled with his own blood. <div eID="gen4530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4531" type="x-p"/> 1. In his agony in the garden. <div eID="gen4531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4532" type="x-p"/> 2. In his being crowned with thorns. <div eID="gen4532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4533" type="x-p"/> 3. In the piercing of his hands and his feet. And, <div eID="gen4533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4534" type="x-p"/> 4. In his side being pierced with the spear. All these were so many acts of atonement performed by the high priest.
entries.56a5b48f7cf73c47957e6911aa573673654ff369: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen4534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4535" type="x-p"/> For seven days shall he consecrate you - This number was the number of perfection among the Hebrews; and the seven days' consecration implied a perfect and full consecration to the sacerdotal office. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.30">Exo 29:30</reference>.
entries.a9f711359decde41aae198aff0e77645a07c676e: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen4535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4536" type="x-p"/> So Aaron and his sons did - This chapter shows the exact fulfillment of the commands delivered to Moses, Exodus 29; and consequently the complete preparation of Aaron and his sons to fill the awfully important office of priests and mediators between God and Israel, to offer sacrifices and make atonement for the sins of the people. "Thus," says Mr. Ainsworth, "the covenant of the priesthood was confirmed unto the tribe of Levi in Aaron and his sons, which covenant was life and peace, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.5">Mal 2:5</reference>. But these are made priests without an oath; also, there were many priests, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death; and they served unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, offering gifts and sacrifices which could not make him who did the service perfect as pertaining to the conscience; for they were carnal ordinances imposed upon them till the time of reformation, that is, until the time of Christ, who was made a priest of God with an oath, and made surety of a better covenant established on better promises. And because he continueth for ever, he hath a priesthood which passeth not from one to another, and is a minister of the true tabernacle, which God pitched and not man. Not by the blood of bulls and of goats, but by his own blood, he entered once into the holy place, having found everlasting redemption for us; and is therefore able to save to the uttermost them who come unto God through him, as he ever liveth to make intercession for them." Taken in reference to his priesthood and sacrifice, all these rites and ceremonies are significant and edifying, but taken out of his relation, they would be as absurd and nugatory as the consecration of the Roman Pontifex Maximus, mentioned above by Prudentius.  <chapter eID="Lev.8"/> <div eID="gen4536" type="x-p"/>

entries.923e2acc074f32f615e2bb681e884198cad0a825: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.1-Lev.8.4">Lev 8:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen1246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1247" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.8.1-Lev.8.5">Lev 8:1-5</reference> contain an account of the preparations for this holy act, the performance of which was enjoined upon Moses by Jehovah after the publication of the laws of sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.1">Lev 8:1</reference>). Moses brought the persons to be consecrated, the official costume that had been made for them (Ex 28), the anointing oil (Exo 30:23.), and the requisite sacrificial offerings (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.3">Exo 29:1-3</reference>), to the door of the tabernacle (i.e., into the court, near the altar of burnt-offering), and then gathered “the whole congregation” - that is to say, the nation in the persons of its elders-there also (see my <hi type="italic">Archäeologie</hi> ii. p. 221). The definite article before the objects enumerated in <reference osisRef="Lev.8.2">Lev 8:2</reference> may be explained on the ground that they had all been previously and more minutely described. The “<hi type="italic">basket of the unleavened</hi>” contained, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.29.2-Exod.3.1">Exo 29:2-3, (1</reference>) unleavened bread, which is called חלּה in <reference osisRef="Lev.8.26">Lev 8:26</reference>, i.e., round flat bread-cakes, and לחם כּכּר (loaf of bread) in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.23">Exo 29:23</reference>, and was baked for the purpose of the consecration (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.8.31">Lev 8:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.32">Lev 8:32</reference>); (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.2">2</reference>) unleavened oil-cakes; and (3) unleavened flat cakes covered with oil (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.4">Lev 2:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Lev 7:12</reference>).
entries.c0add8accaede19c96da3857e5f01cbf7f2df58d: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.5">Lev 8:5</reference> <div eID="gen1247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1248" type="x-p"/> When the congregation was assembled, Moses said, “<hi type="italic">This is the word which Jehovah commanded you to do</hi>.” His meaning was, the substance or essential part of the instructions in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.1">Exo 28:1</reference> and 29:1-37, which he had published to the assembled congregation before the commencement of the act of consecration, and which are not repeated here as being already known from those chapters. The congregation had been summoned to perform this act, because Aaron and his sons were to be consecrated as priests for them, as standing mediators between them and the Lord. <div eID="gen1248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1249" type="x-p"/> After this the act of consecration commenced. It consisted of two parts: first, the consecration of the persons themselves to the office of the priesthood, by washing, clothing, and anointing (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.6-Lev.8.13">Lev 8:6-13</reference>); and secondly, the sacrificial rites, by which the persons appointed to the priestly office were inducted into the functions and prerogatives of priests (vv. 16-36).
entries.ef78174d725797b2032e8832e09bbcaf8b373599: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.6-Lev.8.13">Lev 8:6-13</reference> <div eID="gen1249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1250" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">washing, clothing,</hi> and <hi type="italic">anointing</hi>. - Lev 8:6. “<hi type="italic">Moses brought Aaron and his sons, and washed them with water;</hi>” i.e., directed them to wash themselves, no doubt all over, and not merely their hands and feet. This cleansing from bodily uncleanness was a symbol of the putting away of the filth of sin; the washing of the body, therefore, was a symbol of spiritual cleansing, without which no one could draw near to God, and least of all those who were to perform the duties of reconciliation.
entries.26d69d667f810a5909a64d2f1829e032fbc3b201: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.14-Lev.8.17">Lev 8:14-17</reference> <div eID="gen1253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1254" type="x-p"/> The first sacrifice was a sin-offering, for which a young ox was taken (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.1">Exo 29:1</reference>), as in the case of the sin-offerings for the high priest and the whole congregation (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.14">Lev 4:14</reference>): the highest kind of sacrificial animal, which corresponded to the position to be occupied by the priests in the Israelitish kingdom of God, as the ἐκλογή of the covenant nation. Moses put some of the blood with his finger upon the horns of the altar of burnt-offering, and poured the rest at the foot of the altar. The far portions (see <reference osisRef="Lev.3.3-Lev.3.4">Lev 3:3-4</reference>) he burned upon the altar; but the flesh of the ox, as well as the hide and dung, he burned outside the camp. According to the general rule of the sin-offerings, whose flesh was burnt outside the camp, the blood was brought into the sanctuary itself (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.23">Lev 6:23</reference>); but here it was only put upon the altar of burnt-offering to make this sin-offering a consecration-sacrifice. Moses was to take the blood to “<hi type="italic">purify</hi> (יחטּא) <hi type="italic">and sanctify the altar, to expiate it</hi>.” As the altar had been sanctified immediately before by the anointing with holy oil (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.11">Lev 8:11</reference>), the object of the cleansing or sanctification of it through the blood of the sacrifice cannot have been to purify it a second time from uncleanness, that still adhered to it, or was inherent in it; but just as the purification or expiation of the vessels or worship generally applied only to the sins of the nation, by which these vessels had been defiled (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.16">Lev 16:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.19">Lev 16:19</reference>), so here the purification of the altar with the blood of the sin-offering, upon which the priests had laid their hands, had reference simply to pollutions, with which the priests defiled the altar when officiating at it, through the uncleanness of their sinful nature. As the priests could not be installed in the functions of the priesthood, notwithstanding the holiness communicated to them through the anointing, without a sin-offering to awaken the consciousness in both themselves and the nation that the sinfulness which lay at the root of human nature was not removed by the anointing, but only covered in the presence of the holy God, and that sin still clung to man, and polluted all his doings and designs; so that altar, upon which they were henceforth to offer sacrifices, still required to be purified through the blood of the bullock, that had been slaughtered as a sin-offering for the expiation of their sins, to sanctify it for the service of the priests, i.e., to cover up the sins by which they would defile it when performing their service. For this sanctification the blood of the sin-offering, that had been slaughtered for them, was taken, to indicate the fellowship which was henceforth to exist between them and the altar, and to impress upon them the fact, that the blood, by which they were purified, was also to serve as the means of purifying the altar from the sins attaching to their service. Although none of the blood of this sin-offering was carried into the holy place, because only the anointed priests were to be thereby inducted into the fellowship of the altar, the flesh of the animal could only be burnt outside the camp, because the sacrifice served to purify the priesthood (see <reference osisRef="Lev.4.11-Lev.4.12">Lev 4:11-12</reference>). For the rest, the remarks made on <reference osisRef="Lev.4.4">Lev 4:4</reference> are also applicable to the symbolical meaning of this sacrifice.
entries.008dbff75dddc0f390afdf25d1786539ad7eccc5: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.18-Lev.8.21">Lev 8:18-21</reference> <div eID="gen1254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1255" type="x-p"/> The sin-offering, through which the priests and the altar had been expiated, and every disturbance of the fellowship existing between the holy God and His servants at the altar, in consequence of the sin of those who were to be consecrated, had been taken away, was followed by a burnt-offering, consisting of a ram, which was offered according to the ordinary ritual of the burnt-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.3-Lev.1.9">Lev 1:3-9</reference>), and served to set forth the priests, who had appointed it as their substitute through the laying on of hands, as a living, holy, and well-pleasing sacrifice to the Lord, and to sanctify them to the Lord with all the faculties of both body and soul.
entries.3113225089534bd04cf254abedfc0fef865e653a: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.22-Lev.8.30">Lev 8:22-30</reference> <div eID="gen1255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1256" type="x-p"/> This was followed by the presentation of a peace-offering, which also consisted of a ram, called “<hi type="italic">the ram of the filling,</hi>” or “<hi type="italic">of the fill-offering,</hi>” from the peculiar ceremony performed with the flesh, by which this sacrifice became a consecration-offering, inducting the persons consecrated into the possession and enjoyment of the privileges of the priesthood. A ram was offered as a peace-offering, by the nation as a whole (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.4">Lev 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.18">Lev 9:18</reference>), the tribe-princes (Num 7:17.), and a Nazarite (Num 6:14, Num 6:17), who also occupied a higher position in the congregation (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.11-Amos.2.12">Amo 2:11-12</reference>); but it was never brought by a private Israelite for a peace-offering. The offering described here differed from the rest of the peace-offerings, first of all, in the ceremony performed with the blood (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.23">Lev 8:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.8.24">Lev 8:24</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.29.20-Exod.29.21">Exo 29:20-21</reference>). Before sprinkling the blood upon the altar, Moses put some of it upon the tip of the right ear, upon the right thumb, and upon the great toe of the right foot of Aaron and his sons. Thus he touched the extreme points, which represented the whole, of the ear, hand, and foot on the right, or more important and principal side: the <hi type="italic">ear</hi>, because the priest was always to hearken to the word and commandment of God; the <hi type="italic">hand</hi>, because he was to discharge the priestly functions properly; and the <hi type="italic">foot</hi>, because he was to walk correctly in the sanctuary. Through this manipulation the three organs employed in the priestly service were placed, by means of their tips, <hi type="italic">en rapport</hi> with the sacrificial blood; whilst through the subsequent sprinkling of the blood upon the altar they were introduced symbolically within the sphere of the divine grace, by virtue of the sacrificial blood, which represented the soul as the principle of life, and covered it in the presence of the holiness of God, to be sanctified by that grace to the rendering of willing and righteous service to the Lord. The sanctification was at length completed by Moses’ taking some of the anointing oil and some of the blood upon the altar, and sprinkling Aaron and his sons, and also their clothes; that is to say, by his sprinkling the persons themselves, as bearers of the priesthood, and their clothes, as the insignia of the priesthood, with a mixture of holy anointing oil and sacrificial blood taken from the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.30">Lev 8:30</reference>). The blood taken from the altar shadowed forth the soul as united with God through the medium of the atonement, and filled with powers of grace. The holy anointing oil was a symbol of the Spirit of God. Consequently, through this sprinkling the priests were endowed, both soul and spirit, with the higher powers of the divine life. The sprinkling, however, was performed, not upon the persons alone, but also upon their official dress. For it had reference to the priests, not in their personal or individual relation to the Lord, but in their official position, and with regard to their official work in the congregation of the Lord.<note placement="foot">In the instructions in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.21">Exo 29:21</reference> this ceremony is connected with the sprinkling of the blood upon the altar; but here, on the contrary, it is mentioned after the burning of the flesh. Whether because it was not performed till after this, or because it is merely recorded here in a supplementary form, it is difficult to decide. The latter is the more probable, because the blood upon the altar would soon run off; so that if Moses wanted to take any of it off, it could not be long delayed.</note> <div eID="gen1256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1257" type="x-p"/> In addition to this, the following appointment is contained in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.29">Exo 29:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.30">Exo 29:30</reference> : “The holy garments of Aaron shall be his sons’ after him,” i.e., pass to his successors in the high-priesthood, “to anoint them therein and fill their hands therein. Seven days shall the priest of his sons in his stead put them on (ילבּשׁם with the suffix - ם as in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.19">Gen 19:19</reference>), who shall go into the tabernacle to serve in the sanctuary.” Accordingly, at Aaron’s death his successor Eleazar was dressed in his robes (Num 20:26-28). It by no means follows from this, that a formal priestly consecration was repeated solely in the case of the high priest as the head of the priesthood, and that with the common priests the first anointing by Moses sufficed for all time. We have already observed at p. 545 that this is not involved in <reference osisRef="Exod.40.15">Exo 40:15</reference>; and the fact that it is only the official costume of the high priest which is expressly said to have passed to his successor, may be explained on the simple ground, that as his dress was only worn when he was discharging certain special functions before Jehovah, it would not be worn out so soon as the dress of the ordinary priests, which was worn in the daily service, and therefore would hardly last long enough to be handed down from father to son.<note placement="foot">It no more follows from the omission of express instructions concerning the repetition of the ceremony in the case of every priest who had to be consecrated, that the future priests were not invested, anointed, and in all respects formally consecrated, than the fact that the anointing is not mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.8.13">Lev 8:13</reference> proves that the priests were not anointed at all.</note> <div eID="gen1257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1258" type="x-p"/> The ceremony performed with the flesh of this sacrifice was also peculiarly significant (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.25-Lev.8.29">Lev 8:25-29</reference>). Moses took the fat portions, which were separated from the flesh in the case of the ordinary peace-offerings and burned upon the altar, and the right leg, which was usually assigned to the officiating priest, and then laid by the pieces of flesh (or upon them) another cake of each of the three kinds of pastry, which fell to the portion of the priest in other cases, as a heave-offering for Jehovah, and put all this into the hands of Aaron and his sons, and waved it as a wave-offering for Jehovah, after which he took it from their hands and burned it upon the altar, “<hi type="italic">as a filling</hi> (מלּאים) <hi type="italic">for a savour of satisfaction, as a firing for Jehovah.</hi>” These last words, which are attached to the preceding without a conjunction, and, as the הם and הוּא show, form independent clauses (lit., “<hi type="italic">filling are they...a firing is it for Jehovah</hi>”), contain the reason for this unusual proceeding, so that <hi type="italic">Luther's</hi> explanation is quite correct, “for it is a fill-offering,” etc. The ceremony of handing the portions mentioned to Aaron and his sons denoted the filling of their hands with the sacrificial gifts, which they were afterwards to offer to the Lord in the case of the peace-offerings, viz., the fat portions as a firing upon the altar, the right leg along with the bread-cake as a wave-offering, which the Lord then relinquished to them as His own servants. The filling of their hands with these sacrificial gifts, from which the offering received the name of fill-offering, signified on the one hand the communication of the right belonging to the priest to offer the fat portions to the Lord upon the altar, and on the other hand the enfeoffment of the priests with gifts, which they were to receive in future for their service. This symbolical signification of the act in question serves to explain the circumstance, that both the fat portions, which were to be burned upon the altar, and also the right leg with the bread-cakes which formed the priests’ share of the peace-offerings, were merely placed in the priests’s hands in this instance, and presented symbolically to the Lord by waving, and then burned by Moses upon the altar. For Aaron and his sons were not only to be enfeoffed with what they were to burn unto the Lord, but also with what they would receive for their service. And as even the latter was a prerogative bestowed upon them by the Lord, it was right that at their consecration they should offer it <hi type="italic">symbolically</hi> to the Lord by waving, and <hi type="italic">actually</hi> by burning upon the altar. But as the right leg was devoted to another purpose in this case, Moses received the breast-piece, which was presented to the Lord by waving (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.29">Lev 8:29</reference>), and which afterwards fell to the lot of the priests, as his portion for the sacrificial meal, which formed the conclusion of this dedicatory offering, as it did of all the peace-offerings. In <reference osisRef="Exod.29.27-Exod.29.28">Exo 29:27-28</reference>, we also find the command, that the wave-breast of the ram of the fill-offering, and the heave-leg which had been lifted off, should afterwards belong to Aaron and his sons on the part of the children of Israel, as a perpetual statute, i.e., as a law for all time; and the following reason is assigned: “<hi type="italic">for it is a heave-offering</hi> (<hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, a lifting off), <hi type="italic">and shall be a heave-offering on the part of the children of Israel of their peace-offerings, their heave-offering for Jehovah,</hi>” i.e., which they were to give to the Lord from their peace-offerings for the good of His servants. The application of the word <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> to both kinds of offering, the wave-breast and the heave-shoulder, may be explained on the simple ground, that the gift to be waved had to be lifted off from the sacrificial animal before the waving could be performed.
entries.c59a838edc31457d1ab73df479c2782e7d0e4ef7: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.31-Lev.8.32">Lev 8:31-32</reference> <div eID="gen1258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1259" type="x-p"/> For the sacrificial meal, the priests were to boil the flesh in front of the door of the tabernacle, or, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.29.31">Exo 29:31</reference>, “at the holy place,” i.e., in the court, and eat it with the bread in the fill-offering basket; and no stranger (i.e., layman or non-priest) was to take part in the meal, because the flesh and bread were holy (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.33">Exo 29:33</reference>), that is to say, had served to make atonement for the priests, to fill their hands and sanctify them. Atoning virtue is attributed to this sacrifice in the same sense as to the burnt-offering in Lev 1:4. Whatever was left of the flesh and bread until the following day, that is to say, was not eaten on the day of sacrifice, was to be burned with fire, for the reason explained at Lev 7:17. The exclusion of laymen from participating in this sacrificial meal is to be accounted for in the same way as the prohibition of unleavened bread, which was offered and eaten in the case of the ordinary peace-offerings along with the unleavened sacrificial cakes (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.13">Lev 7:13</reference>). The meal brought the consecration of the priests to a close, as Aaron and his sons were thereby received into that special, priestly covenant with the Lord, the blessings and privileges of which were to be enjoyed by the consecrated priests alone. At this meal the priests were not allowed to eat leavened bread, any more than the nation generally at the feast of Passover (Exo 12:8.).
entries.2cd95b0f8800a8f4046a35a48d789b3460c9c9e1: <reference osisRef="Lev.8.33-Lev.8.36">Lev 8:33-36</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.29.35-Exod.29.37">Exo 29:35-37</reference>). The consecration was to last seven days, during which time the persons to be consecrated were not to go away from the door of the tabernacle, but to remain there day and night, and watch the watch of the Lord that they might not die. “<hi type="italic">For the Lord will fill your hand seven days. As they have done on this</hi> (the first) <hi type="italic">day, so has Jehovah commanded to do to make atonement for you</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.34">Lev 8:34</reference>). That is to say, the rite of consecration which has been performed upon you to-day, Jehovah has commanded to be performed or repeated for seven days. These words clearly imply that the whole ceremony, in all its details, was to be repeated for seven days; and in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.36-Exod.29.37">Exo 29:36-37</reference>, besides the filling of the hand which was to be continued seven days, and which presupposes the daily repetition of the consecration-offering, the preparation of the sin-offering for reconciliation and the expiation or purification and anointing of the altar are expressly commanded for each of the seven days. This repetition of the act of consecration is to be regarded as intensifying the consecration itself; and the limitation of it to seven days is to be accounted for from the signification and holiness of the number seven as the sign of the completion of the works of God. The commandment not to leave the court of the tabernacle during the whole seven days, is of course not to be understood literally (as it is by some of the Rabbins), as meaning that the persons to be consecrated were not even to go away from the spot for the necessities of nature (cf. <hi type="italic">Lund. jüd. Heiligth.</hi> p. 448); but when taken in connection with the clause which follows, “<hi type="italic">and keep the charge of the Lord,</hi>” it can only be understood as signifying that during these days they were not to leave the sanctuary to attend to any earthly avocation whatever, but uninterruptedly to observe the charge of the Lord, i.e., the consecration commanded by the Lord. משׁמרת שׁמר, lit., to watch the watch of a person or thing, i.e., to attend to them, to do whatever was required for noticing or attending to them (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.26.5">Gen 26:5</reference>, and Hengstenberg, Christology).  <chapter eID="Lev.8"/> <div eID="gen1259" type="x-p"/>

1. And the Lord spake. It is well known that in conjunction with the sacrifices there was an offering, which they call minha, but we shall elsewhere see that this was also used separately; for it was lawful without a victim to offer either plain meal, or cakes, or wafers seasoned with oil. Therefore, besides the sacrifice of consecration, of which Moses has already treated, this second offering is required from the priest, that he should present at his inauguration a cake fried in a pan, and cut in pieces. The reason of this appears to have been, that he might thence become the legitimate minister of all the people, and might duly offer in the name of others, when he had done what was right for himself. But a distinction is drawn between the demand upon the priest and that, upon the people, viz., that it should be “wholly burnt;” the reason for which, since it will be explained elsewhere, it will be now sufficient to advert to in a single word. The fact was that God was unwilling that the priests should indulge themselves in vain ostentation, which might have been easily the case, if the oblation had been preserved for their use, like the minha of the people which remained in their hands.

entries.a0128880e29c50c05fdd1a36daac95457038407f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.8.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.8.4" sID="gen18247" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen18248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4. </hi><hi type="italic">And Moses did as the Lord commanded him</hi> Although these things relate to the priesthood, the authority and nature of which I expounded under the Second Commandment, yet, inasmuch as they are historical, it is not without reason that I have thought fit to defer them till this place: for, if I had referred to them in connection with the Commandment, unpractised readers would not have easily taken notice of their time. This distinction, however, will be of great assistance to them, that after the doctrine which was properly contained in the Decalogue has been set forth, they will now see how faithfully Moses fulfilled whatever he was commanded, and will be able to compare his obedience with the injunction, as they have done in the whole of the making and dedication of the tabernacle. Besides, there is no question but that the narrative must be thus connected; for it may be readily inferred from many passages, that the priests were anointed on the same day that the tabernacle was consecrated. I will now hastily run through the words. Moses says that he brought near Aaron and his sons, <hi type="italic">i.e.,</hi> to set them before God and the people; and then that he “washed them with water,” to make it manifest that they did not bring from their homes the purity which befitted the sanctity of their office, and, inasmuch as they were men, that they could not be clean before God, unless their impurity was washed off. A description of their apparel afterwards follows, which I pass over, lest I should weary my readers by twice repeating the same thing.<div eID="gen18248" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.8.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen18247" osisID="Lev.8.4" type="section"/>

10. And Moses took the anointing oil I have stated why God commanded that the priest himself, as well as all the vessels, should be consecrated with oil, viz., because, without the influence of the Spirit, all the sacrifices would be unsavory. And it is by the operation of the same Spirit that Christ was made the peace-maker between God and men; because this dignity would not otherwise belong to flesh and human nature. Aaron was therefore anointed, together with his sons, before he was admitted to the priestly office; for it is afterwards added, that “the bullock for sin”
“For the sin-offering.” — A. V.
was brought, upon which Aaron laid his hands. Now, although even then he began to discharge his office, yet Moses still occupied the first place, and performed, as it were, the final act. Hence it was that he sprinkled the horns of the altar with the blood; poured the residue at its base for expiation; and burned the sacrifice upon the altar. Now, the imposition of hands in the sacrifices was not only a symbol of presentation, but also a testimony of guilt transferred to the victim. Since, however, this last statement may be obscure on account of its brevity, I will explain it a little more clearly. If any private person offered a victim, the imposition of hands signified that he cast the guilt of his sin upon the victim. Hence the name of piaculum;
“Et voyla pourquoy les bestes ont porte le nom d’offense;” and behold wherefore the beasts bore the name of offence. — Fr. “Piaculum; sacrum piaculare, et quicquid ad piandum et purgandum pertinet. Metonymice, ipsa res, qum piaculi causa adhibetur; sic AEn. 6:153.
Duc nigos pecudes: ea prima piacula sunto.” — Facciolati.
because it sustained the curse of God, and was substituted in the sinner’s stead, who disburdens himself upon it of whatever exposed him to the judgment of God. But, inasmuch as common hands were unworthy to consecrate a victim to God, the sacerdotal office interposed. This is the reason why Aaron and his sons put their hands on each of the sacrifices, in order that this kind of atonement (piaculi) might be the beginning of their consecration, which was completed in the second ram, with the blood of which Moses stained their right ears, the thumbs of their right hands, and the great toes of their right feet. A multitude of questions here arises: Why only one side of the priests was consecrated, as if their left side remained polluted? Why consecration was not also imparted to their eyes, and especially to their mouth, which was to be the organ of the Holy Spirit? But this warning must be always borne in mind, that we should be soberly wise in those points, the certain knowledge of which cannot be elicited from Scripture; for our curiosity is not only frivolous, but also perverse and injurious, when we desire to know more than God has revealed. The conjecture, however, is probable, that the whole body was consecrated in the right side. We have already seen elsewhere,
See ante, vol. 2, p. 211.
that by the hands and feet the whole life and actions of men are designated. In which view the cleanness of the heart and the purity of the hands comprehend all that is internal and external in man, as the root and the fruit. As to the feet, the metaphor of walking is notorious; and the feet are said to run to evil, and to be swift to shed blood, when the wicked and the despisers of God betake themselves to evil deeds. Besides, since this consecration was not to the office of teaching, but to that of intercession, the ear rather than the tongue is stained with blood; because the chief virtue, which obtains grace in the sacrifices, is obedience. To this the passage in Psalm 40:6, refers, “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou bored:”
A. V., “Mine ears hast thou opened.” Margin, “Heb., digged.” See C.’s translation and note. Cal. Soc. edit., vol. 2, p. 99.
to which the words of Jeremiah correspond,
“Did I command anything respecting sacrifices, and not rather that your fathers should obey my voice?”
This quotation is much abbreviated. C.’s exposition of the passage, (Cal. Soc. edit., vol. 1, p. 393,) and Mr. Owen’s note, are worthy of consultation.
(Jeremiah 7:22, 23.)
And hence Moses commenced the consecration at the ear, in order to devote the priest to God unto obedience. Paul shews how this was fulfilled in Christ, where he celebrates His obedience in the sacrifice of His death, in order to reconcile His Father to us. (Romans 5:19.) I have spoken elsewhere of the kind of wave-offering which they called tnupha.

31. And Moses said unto Aaron and his sons, Boil the flesh This is the universal rule, as we have seen elsewhere.
See ante, vol. 2, p. 133.
One thing only is special, that God kept them in the tabernacle seven days, that they might learn to subordinate all their domestic cares and worldly business to their sacred duties. It has been elsewhere said, also,
Ibid., p.26.
that perfection is denoted by the number seven, which this passage confirms, for by the seven days they were reminded that they were no longer their own masters for the rest of their life.

                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And Moses said unto Aaron, and to his sons, Boil the flesh <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That which was left of the ram, and particularly the breast, which was said to be <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his part, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 29. and by him was given to <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> that he and his sons might eat of it in token that they and onely they should have the right to do so for the future.</ns0:note> at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation: and there <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 29. 32.</ns0:note> eat it with the bread that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the basket of consecrations, as I commanded, saying, Aaron and his sons shall eat it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And that which remaineth of the flesh, and of the bread, shall ye burn with fire.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And ye shall not go out of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> seven dayes, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />till the dayes of your consecration be at an end: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 29. 30, 35.</ns0:note> seven dayes <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">In which the same ceremonies were to be repeated, as the next verse implies<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and other rites to be performed.</ns0:note> shall he <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther God; or <ns0:hi>

                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> for the words may be spoken by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> either in Gods name or in his own<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>

                  <ns0:p n="34">34 As he hath done this day, <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> the LORD hath commanded to do, to make an atonement for you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 Therefore shall ye abide at the door of the congregation day and night seven dayes, and keep the charge of the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">What God hath commanded you concerning your conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cration.</ns0:note>, that ye die not <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">If the threatning seem too severe for the fault, it must be considered both that it is the usual practise of Lawgi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers most severely to punish the first offences for the terrour and caution of others and for the maintenance of their own authority; and that this transgression was aggravated by many circumstances, being committed by sacred and eminent persons and that in the presence of the people<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which made it a publick scandal, and in Gods worship, where he is very tender and jea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lous, and against a plain and easie command of God, and at a time when they were receiving high favours and priviledges from God. Nor is sin to be esteemed or measured by the idle fancies of men of corrupt minds and lives, whose interests and lusts easily blind their minds, but by the Authority, Majesty, and Will of the great, and wise, and iust Lawgiver.</ns0:note>, for so I am commanded.</ns0:p>
